# Pain relief with opium and willow bark (laudanum, morphine, aspirin) (`opium_analgesia`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by distillation, synthetic_dyes
- Core idea: Opium is dried poppy latex containing morphine and other alkaloids. It can relieve severe pain, but the same drugs can suppress breathing and cause fatal overdose. Laudanum was a historical tincture; neither a drop count nor appearance establishes the strength of a homemade preparation. Alcohol adds to respiratory depression. Repeated use can cause tolerance and physical dependence, and withdrawal can follow abrupt cessation. Willow bark contains salicylates, which act differently. Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, a manufactured drug that can also cause bleeding.
- Pitfalls:
  - Dosing opium by guess; the gap between relief and death is small, and smaller with wine
  - Laudanum to quieten babies, which killed many children
  - Calling willow bark 'natural aspirin' and expecting tablet strength; a cup of bark tea holds very little
  - Giving aspirin-like drugs to bleeding patients
  - Repeating that ancient Egyptians and Hippocrates used willow as a painkiller; the textual evidence is thin
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3000 BC – a Sumerian sign often read as 'joy plant' may mean the poppy (disputed); egypt: c. 1550 BC – Ebers papyrus: poppy remedy to stop children crying; greece: 1st c. AD – Dioscorides describes how to score poppy capsules and collect opium, and warns of overdose; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's Canon gives opium's uses and dangers; Arab traders carry it east; china: 7th–8th c. – poppy known as medicine; opium smoking spreads in the 17th–18th c.; europe: 1660s – Sydenham's laudanum; 1763 Edward Stone reports willow bark for agues; 1804–1817 Sertürner isolates morphine; 1828 salicin; 1853 hypodermic syringe (Pravaz, Wood); 1897–1899 aspirin at Bayer (credit disputed between Hoffmann and Eichengrün)
- Read:
  - Friedrich Sertürner, Ueber das Morphium, eine neue salzfähige Grundlage, und die Mekonsäure, Annalen der Physik (1817)
  - Martin Booth, Opium: A History (1996)
  - Diarmuid Jeffreys, Aspirin: The Remarkable Story of a Wonder Drug (2004)
